claim: Inhibition of lysosomal acidification triggers cellular iron deficiency.
source: We show here that inhibition of lysosomal acidification triggers cellular iron deficiency, which results in impaired mitochondrial function and non-apoptotic cell death.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing decreased Fe2+ levels in bafilomycin-treated cells (Figure 1F), increased Tfrc expression, and decreased ferritin levels (Figure 2A).

claim: Iron deficiency caused by lysosomal acidification impairment results in impaired mitochondrial function.
source: We show here that inhibition of lysosomal acidification triggers cellular iron deficiency, which results in impaired mitochondrial function and non-apoptotic cell death.
evidence: Demonstrated by decreased mitochondrial oxygen consumption rates in bafilomycin-treated cells (Figure 3B-C) and decreased mitochondrial Fe2+ levels (Figure 3A).

claim: Iron deficiency caused by lysosomal acidification impairment results in non-apoptotic cell death.
source: We show here that inhibition of lysosomal acidification triggers cellular iron deficiency, which results in impaired mitochondrial function and non-apoptotic cell death.
evidence: Supported by cell death assays showing no cleaved caspase-3 or cleaved PARP in bafilomycin-treated cells (Figure 4F), and cell death not prevented by pan-caspase inhibitor ZVAD (Figure 4G).

claim: Supplying iron via a lysosome-independent pathway recovers the effects of lysosomal acidification inhibition.
source: These effects are recovered by supplying iron via a lysosome-independent pathway.
evidence: Demonstrated by Fe-citrate supplementation restoring HIF-1α levels (Figure 2D), mitochondrial respiration (Figure 3B-C), and cell viability (Figure 4C) in bafilomycin-treated cells.

claim: Iron deficiency is sufficient to trigger inflammatory signaling in cultured primary neurons.
source: Notably, iron deficiency is sufficient to trigger inflammatory signaling in cultured primary neurons.
evidence: Shown by increased expression of Tnfa, innate immune regulators (Tlr9, Myd88, Irf7, Stat1, Stat2), and interferon-stimulated genes (Cxcl10, Isg15, Ifit1, Ifit3, Ifi44) in deferoxamine-treated primary neurons (Figure 4I-K).

claim: A mouse model of impaired lysosomal acidification shows a robust iron deficiency response in the brain.
source: Using a mouse model of impaired lysosomal acidification, we observed a robust iron deficiency response in the brain, verified by in vivo magnetic resonance imaging.
evidence: Demonstrated by increased Tfrc transcript levels, decreased FTL1 protein levels, and HIF-1α accumulation in Gaa-KO mouse cortex (Figure 5A-C), and decreased T2 relaxation times by MRI (Table 1).

claim: The brains of Gaa-KO mice present a pervasive inflammatory signature.
source: Furthermore, the brains of these mice present a pervasive inflammatory signature associated with instability of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), both corrected by supplementation of the mice diet with iron.
evidence: Shown by RNA sequencing revealing enrichment of inflammation-related pathways (Figure 6C), activation of Irf7 and Irf3 (Figure 6D-E), increased expression of interferon-stimulated genes (Figure 6F), and increased GFAP levels (Figure 6G-H).

claim: The inflammatory signature in Gaa-KO mouse brains is associated with instability of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA).
source: Furthermore, the brains of these mice present a pervasive inflammatory signature associated with instability of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), both corrected by supplementation of the mice diet with iron.
evidence: Demonstrated by age-dependent decline in mtDNA copy number in Gaa-KO cortex (Figure 7A) and reduced TFAM protein levels (Figure 7B).

claim: Iron supplementation in the diet corrects the inflammatory signature in Gaa-KO mouse brains.
source: Furthermore, the brains of these mice present a pervasive inflammatory signature associated with instability of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), both corrected by supplementation of the mice diet with iron.
evidence: Shown by iron-enriched diet dampening increased expression of innate immune response genes (Figure 7E), reducing GFAP and TNFα protein levels (Figure 7F), and normalizing cytokine levels (Figure 7G) in Gaa-KO mice.

claim: Iron supplementation in the diet corrects mtDNA instability in Gaa-KO mouse brains.
source: Furthermore, the brains of these mice present a pervasive inflammatory signature associated with instability of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), both corrected by supplementation of the mice diet with iron.
evidence: Demonstrated by iron-enriched diet rescuing mtDNA copy number defects in 2-month-old Gaa-KO mice (Figure 7D).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment of cells results in HIF-1α accumulation.
source: Notably, the protein levels of HIF-1α were increased in bafilomycin (or Baf in figures)-treated fibroblasts (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown by immunoblot of HIF-1α in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 1D).

claim: Saliphenylhalamide treatment of cells results in HIF-1α accumulation.
source: A similar result was obtained in fibroblasts treated with a different inhibitor of the lysosomal v-ATPase, saliphenylhalamide (henceforth, saliphe [or Sal in figures]) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown by immunoblot of HIF-1α in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 1D).

claim: VHL protein levels are not changed in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: The protein levels of VHL were not changed in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown by immunoblot of VHL in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 1D).

claim: Cell-permeant α-ketoglutarate supplementation does not decrease HIF-1α accumulation in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: To test if the reason why HIF-1α was accumulating upon v-ATPase inhibition was due to decreased levels of α-ketoglutarate, we added a cell-permeant form of α-ketoglutarate to the bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts, and found no decrease in the accumulation of HIF-1α (Figure 1E).
evidence: Shown by immunoblot of HIF-1α in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with α-ketoglutarate supplementation (Figure 1E).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment results in decreased total, Fe2+, and Fe3+ levels in fibroblasts.
source: Then, we tested if there were any perturbations in Fe levels. We therefore assessed the total, Fe2+ and Fe3+ levels in bafilomycin-treated and control fibroblasts, and found a robust decrease in total, Fe2+ and Fe3+ (Figure 1E).
evidence: Shown by iron assay measurements in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 1F).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment results in increased lysosomal iron content.
source: Using these purified lysosomes, we measured their total iron content, and found a robust increase in lysosomal iron in the bafilomycin-treated cells (Figure 1I) in agreement with the retention of iron in lysosomes following impaired lysosomal acidification.
evidence: Shown by iron assay measurements in purified lysosomes from bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 1I).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment increases Tfrc transcript levels in fibroblasts.
source: We observed in fibroblasts treated with the v-ATPase inhibitors, bafilomycin and saliphe, increased Tfrc transcript levels and decreased protein amounts of FTL1 and FTH1 (Figure 2).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfrc in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 2A).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment decreases FTL1 and FTH1 protein levels in fibroblasts.
source: We observed in fibroblasts treated with the v-ATPase inhibitors, bafilomycin and saliphe, increased Tfrc transcript levels and decreased protein amounts of FTL1 and FTH1 (Figure 2).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of FTL1 and FTH1 in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 2A).

claim: Saliphenylhalamide treatment increases Tfrc transcript levels in fibroblasts.
source: We observed in fibroblasts treated with the v-ATPase inhibitors, bafilomycin and saliphe, increased Tfrc transcript levels and decreased protein amounts of FTL1 and FTH1 (Figure 2).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfrc in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 2A).

claim: Saliphenylhalamide treatment decreases FTL1 and FTH1 protein levels in fibroblasts.
source: We observed in fibroblasts treated with the v-ATPase inhibitors, bafilomycin and saliphe, increased Tfrc transcript levels and decreased protein amounts of FTL1 and FTH1 (Figure 2).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of FTL1 and FTH1 in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 2A).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment decreases FerroOrange signal intensity in fibroblasts.
source: Furthermore, we stained fibroblasts with the probe FerroOrange, which reacts specifically with Fe2+ but not Fe3+, and found that the signal intensity of FerroOrange was sharply decreased in bafilomycin-treated cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown by FerroOrange staining in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 2B).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation deactivates the iron-deficiency response in v-ATPase inhibitor-treated fibroblasts.
source: When fibroblasts are treated simultaneously with v-ATPase inhibitors and Fe-citrate, the iron-deficiency response is deactivated, as assessed by the transcript levels of Tfrc (Figure 2C).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfrc in bafilomycin or saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 2C).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation restores HIF-1α to barely detectable levels in v-ATPase inhibitor-treated fibroblasts.
source: To directly test if the accumulation of HIF-1α upon v-ATPase inhibition was due to the perturbation in Fe homeostasis, we supplemented the growth medium of the bafilomycin- or saliphe-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate, which restored HIF-1α to the barely detectable amounts observed in control cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of HIF-1α in bafilomycin or saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 2D).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation normalizes ferritin levels in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: The striking normalization of ferritin levels upon Fe-citrate supplementation of bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts further underscores that Fe-citrate is being taken up by the cells and resolves the iron deficiency (Figure 2D).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of FTH1 in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 2D).

claim: Transcript levels of HIF-1α targets are robustly induced in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: We observed that the transcript levels of HIF-1α targets are robustly induced in bafilomycin- and saliphe-treated fibroblasts, and are restored to basal levels when the cells are co-treated with v-ATPase inhibitors and Fe-citrate (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of HIF-1α target genes in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 2E).

claim: Transcript levels of HIF-1α targets are robustly induced in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts.
source: We observed that the transcript levels of HIF-1α targets are robustly induced in bafilomycin- and saliphe-treated fibroblasts, and are restored to basal levels when the cells are co-treated with v-ATPase inhibitors and Fe-citrate (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of HIF-1α target genes in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation restores transcript levels of HIF-1α targets to basal levels in v-ATPase inhibitor-treated fibroblasts.
source: We observed that the transcript levels of HIF-1α targets are robustly induced in bafilomycin- and saliphe-treated fibroblasts, and are restored to basal levels when the cells are co-treated with v-ATPase inhibitors and Fe-citrate (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of HIF-1α target genes in bafilomycin or saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts show impaired lysosomal acidification.
source: The Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts show impaired lysosomal acidification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Shown by Dextran-Oregon Green and Dextran-TMRM staining in Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G).

claim: Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts show increased expression of Tfrc.
source: In the Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts we observed increased expression of Tfrc, decreased protein levels of FTH1 and FTL1, and accumulation of HIF-1α (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), as well as increased transcript levels of most HIF-1α target genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfrc in Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts show decreased protein levels of FTH1 and FTL1.
source: In the Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts we observed increased expression of Tfrc, decreased protein levels of FTH1 and FTL1, and accumulation of HIF-1α (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), as well as increased transcript levels of most HIF-1α target genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of FTH1 and FTL1 in Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts show accumulation of HIF-1α.
source: In the Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts we observed increased expression of Tfrc, decreased protein levels of FTH1 and FTL1, and accumulation of HIF-1α (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), as well as increased transcript levels of most HIF-1α target genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of HIF-1α in Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts show increased transcript levels of most HIF-1α target genes.
source: In the Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts we observed increased expression of Tfrc, decreased protein levels of FTH1 and FTL1, and accumulation of HIF-1α (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), as well as increased transcript levels of most HIF-1α target genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of HIF-1α target genes in Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).

claim: Gaa-KO fibroblasts show impaired lysosomal acidification.
source: We assessed lysosomal pH in the Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 2F) and observed impaired acidification, albeit less robust than observed when inhibiting the vATPase or silencing Atp6v1h (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: Shown by Dextran-Oregon Green and Dextran-TMRM staining in Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 2F-G).

claim: Gaa-KO fibroblasts present iron deficiency as shown by increased Tfrc transcript level and decreased FTL1 levels.
source: The Gaa-KO fibroblasts present iron deficiency as shown by increased Tfrc transcript level, and decreased FTL1 levels (Figure 2H).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfrc and immunoblots of FTL1 in Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 2H).

claim: Gaa-KO fibroblasts present HIF-1α accumulation.
source: Notably, these fibroblasts also present HIF-1α accumulation (Figure 2H).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of HIF-1α in Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 2H).

claim: Gaa-KO fibroblasts show a decrease in Fe2+.
source: Furthermore, the Gaa-KO fibroblasts show a decrease in Fe2+ (Figure 2I), in agreement with the iron deficiency response and the accumulation of HIF-1α.
evidence: Shown by iron assay measurements in Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 2I).

claim: Gaa-KO fibroblasts show an increase in Fe3+.
source: The increase in Fe3+ suggests a defect in the endolysosomal reduction of Fe3+ to Fe2+.
evidence: Shown by iron assay measurements in Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 2I).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment results in decreased Mito-FerroGreen signal in fibroblasts.
source: The cells treated with bafilomycin showed a robust decrease in Mito-FerroGreen signal (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown by Mito-FerroGreen staining in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3A).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation restores Mito-FerroGreen signal in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: This effect was ablated in the presence of Fe-citrate (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown by Mito-FerroGreen staining in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 3A).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment results in decreased mitochondrial oxygen consumption in fibroblasts.
source: We observed that fibroblasts treated with either v-ATPase inhibitor bafilomycin or saliphe showed a robust decrease in mitochondrial O2 consumption (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown by Seahorse measurements of oxygen consumption rate in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Saliphenylhalamide treatment results in decreased mitochondrial oxygen consumption in fibroblasts.
source: We observed that fibroblasts treated with either v-ATPase inhibitor bafilomycin or saliphe showed a robust decrease in mitochondrial O2 consumption (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown by Seahorse measurements of oxygen consumption rate in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Deferoxamine treatment results in virtual absence of mitochondrial respiratory chain activity in fibroblasts.
source: Interestingly, treatment of fibroblasts with the lysosomal iron chelator deferoxamine resulted in virtual absence of mitochondrial respiratory chain activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown by Seahorse measurements of oxygen consumption rate in deferoxamine-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation restores mitochondrial respiratory chain activity to normal levels in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: Notably, supplementation of the medium with Fe-citrate was sufficient to return mitochondrial respiratory chain activity to normal levels in cells treated with bafilomycin (Figure 3B), saliphe (Figure 3C) or with deferoxamine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown by Seahorse measurements of oxygen consumption rate in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 3B).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation restores mitochondrial respiratory chain activity to normal levels in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts.
source: Notably, supplementation of the medium with Fe-citrate was sufficient to return mitochondrial respiratory chain activity to normal levels in cells treated with bafilomycin (Figure 3B), saliphe (Figure 3C) or with deferoxamine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown by Seahorse measurements of oxygen consumption rate in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 3C).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation restores mitochondrial respiratory chain activity to normal levels in deferoxamine-treated fibroblasts.
source: Notably, supplementation of the medium with Fe-citrate was sufficient to return mitochondrial respiratory chain activity to normal levels in cells treated with bafilomycin (Figure 3B), saliphe (Figure 3C) or with deferoxamine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown by Seahorse measurements of oxygen consumption rate in deferoxamine-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: v-ATPase inhibition decreases protein levels of respiratory chain subunits in fibroblasts.
source: First, we assessed the protein levels of respiratory chain subunits in whole cell extracts by Western blot, and observed that they are decreased when v-ATPase is inhibited (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of OXPHOS subunits in bafilomycin or saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3D).

claim: v-ATPase inhibition decreases protein levels of VDAC1 and Tom20 in fibroblasts.
source: To assess mitochondrial mass, we measured the protein levels of the proteins VDAC1 and Tom20, which are highly abundant in the outer mitochondrial membrane. We found a decrease in VDAC1 and Tom20 levels in v-ATPase-inhibited cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of VDAC1 and Tom20 in bafilomycin or saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: v-ATPase inhibition results in mitochondrial fragmentation and swelling.
source: Next, we tested if the mitochondrial network was affected by v-ATPase inhibition, and observed a robust phenotype of mitochondrial fragmentation and swelling (Figure 3E).
evidence: Shown by GFP-Mito imaging in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3E).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment results in down-regulation of transcript levels of mitochondrial respiratory chain subunits.
source: We measured the transcript levels of several mitochondrial respiratory chain subunits (all encoded in the nuclear DNA), and found that they all presented a robust down-regulation when treated with bafilomycin (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), or with saliphe (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).

claim: Saliphenylhalamide treatment results in down-regulation of transcript levels of mitochondrial respiratory chain subunits.
source: We measured the transcript levels of several mitochondrial respiratory chain subunits (all encoded in the nuclear DNA), and found that they all presented a robust down-regulation when treated with bafilomycin (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), or with saliphe (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation restores transcript levels of mitochondrial respiratory chain subunits to control levels in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: Notably, supplementation of the cell medium with Fe-citrate returned the transcript levels of the mitochondrial respiratory chain subunits to control levels in bafilomycin (Figure 3G) or saliphe treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 3G).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation restores transcript levels of mitochondrial respiratory chain subunits to control levels in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts.
source: Notably, supplementation of the cell medium with Fe-citrate returned the transcript levels of the mitochondrial respiratory chain subunits to control levels in bafilomycin (Figure 3G) or saliphe treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment results in increased mitochondrial superoxide levels in fibroblasts.
source: Using the mitochondria-targeted superoxide-sensitive dye MitoSox, we observed a sharp increase in MitoSox levels in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts, almost completely recovered in the fibroblasts that also received Fe-citrate (Figure 3H).
evidence: Shown by MitoSox staining in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3H).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation recovers mitochondrial superoxide levels in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: Using the mitochondria-targeted superoxide-sensitive dye MitoSox, we observed a sharp increase in MitoSox levels in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts, almost completely recovered in the fibroblasts that also received Fe-citrate (Figure 3H).
evidence: Shown by MitoSox staining in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 3H).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment results in increased levels of reactive oxygen species in fibroblasts.
source: We probed the levels of pro-oxidant molecules (superoxide, hydroxyl radical, among others) using the probe dichlorofluoresceine (DCF), which reacts with many reactive oxygen species (ROS). We observed a sharp increase in DCF intensity in bafilomycin-treated cells, which was normalized by co-treatment with Fe-citrate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Shown by DCF staining in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation normalizes levels of reactive oxygen species in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: We probed the levels of pro-oxidant molecules (superoxide, hydroxyl radical, among others) using the probe dichlorofluoresceine (DCF), which reacts with many reactive oxygen species (ROS). We observed a sharp increase in DCF intensity in bafilomycin-treated cells, which was normalized by co-treatment with Fe-citrate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Shown by DCF staining in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment results in increased lipid peroxidation in fibroblasts.
source: A similar pattern is observed with the dye BODIPY C11, which reports the levels of oxidized membrane phospholipids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Shown by BODIPY C11 staining in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation normalizes lipid peroxidation in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: A similar pattern is observed with the dye BODIPY C11, which reports the levels of oxidized membrane phospholipids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Shown by BODIPY C11 staining in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).

claim: Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts show decreased mitochondrial respiratory chain activity.
source: Using the Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts, we observed a robust decrease in their mitochondrial respiratory chain activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), decreased protein levels of several OXPHOS subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) and decreased mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Shown by Seahorse measurements of oxygen consumption rate in Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts show decreased protein levels of OXPHOS subunits.
source: Using the Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts, we observed a robust decrease in their mitochondrial respiratory chain activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), decreased protein levels of several OXPHOS subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) and decreased mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of OXPHOS subunits in Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts show decreased mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: Using the Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts, we observed a robust decrease in their mitochondrial respiratory chain activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), decreased protein levels of several OXPHOS subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) and decreased mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes in Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Loss of Mcoln1 triggers an increase in Tfrc transcript levels in fibroblasts.
source: The individual loss of Mcoln1 or Slc11a2, as well as the simultaneous loss of both, triggered an increase in the transcript levels of Tfrc (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) and a decrease in the protein levels of FTL1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfrc in Mcoln1-KO fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Silencing of Slc11a2 triggers an increase in Tfrc transcript levels in fibroblasts.
source: The individual loss of Mcoln1 or Slc11a2, as well as the simultaneous loss of both, triggered an increase in the transcript levels of Tfrc (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) and a decrease in the protein levels of FTL1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfrc in Slc11a2-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Loss of Mcoln1 and silencing of Slc11a2 together trigger an increase in Tfrc transcript levels in fibroblasts.
source: The individual loss of Mcoln1 or Slc11a2, as well as the simultaneous loss of both, triggered an increase in the transcript levels of Tfrc (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) and a decrease in the protein levels of FTL1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfrc in Mcoln1-KO fibroblasts with Slc11a2 silencing (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Loss of Mcoln1 triggers a decrease in FTL1 protein levels in fibroblasts.
source: The individual loss of Mcoln1 or Slc11a2, as well as the simultaneous loss of both, triggered an increase in the transcript levels of Tfrc (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) and a decrease in the protein levels of FTL1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of FTL1 in Mcoln1-KO fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Silencing of Slc11a2 triggers a decrease in FTL1 protein levels in fibroblasts.
source: The individual loss of Mcoln1 or Slc11a2, as well as the simultaneous loss of both, triggered an increase in the transcript levels of Tfrc (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) and a decrease in the protein levels of FTL1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of FTL1 in Slc11a2-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Loss of Mcoln1 and silencing of Slc11a2 together trigger a decrease in FTL1 protein levels in fibroblasts.
source: The individual loss of Mcoln1 or Slc11a2, as well as the simultaneous loss of both, triggered an increase in the transcript levels of Tfrc (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) and a decrease in the protein levels of FTL1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of FTL1 in Mcoln1-KO fibroblasts with Slc11a2 silencing (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Mitochondrial respiration is robustly inhibited in the absence of Mcoln1 and/or Slc11a2.
source: Mitochondrial respiration was robustly inhibited in the absence of Mcoln1 and/or Slc11a2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F), which was underscored by the decrease in the protein levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G) and transcript levels of OXPHOS subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: Shown by Seahorse measurements of oxygen consumption rate in Mcoln1-KO and/or Slc11a2-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).

claim: Loss of Mcoln1 and/or Slc11a2 results in decreased protein levels of OXPHOS subunits.
source: Mitochondrial respiration was robustly inhibited in the absence of Mcoln1 and/or Slc11a2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F), which was underscored by the decrease in the protein levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G) and transcript levels of OXPHOS subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of OXPHOS subunits in Mcoln1-KO and/or Slc11a2-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).

claim: Loss of Mcoln1 and/or Slc11a2 results in decreased transcript levels of OXPHOS subunits.
source: Mitochondrial respiration was robustly inhibited in the absence of Mcoln1 and/or Slc11a2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F), which was underscored by the decrease in the protein levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G) and transcript levels of OXPHOS subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes in Mcoln1-KO and/or Slc11a2-silenced fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).

claim: Bafilomycin treatment results in halting of cell proliferation and cell death in fibroblasts.
source: We observed that fibroblasts treated with vehicle control proliferate, while both bafilomycin (Figure 4A) and saliphe treatments (Figure 4B) resulted not only in halting of cell proliferation but also in cell death (the number of cells decreases during the treatment).
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4A).

claim: Saliphenylhalamide treatment results in halting of cell proliferation and cell death in fibroblasts.
source: We observed that fibroblasts treated with vehicle control proliferate, while both bafilomycin (Figure 4A) and saliphe treatments (Figure 4B) resulted not only in halting of cell proliferation but also in cell death (the number of cells decreases during the treatment).
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4B).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation restores cellular proliferation in v-ATPase inhibitor-treated fibroblasts.
source: Remarkably, the supplementation of the medium with Fe-citrate during v-ATPase inhibition restores cellular proliferation (Figure 4C).
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin or saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 4C).

claim: Antimycin A treatment ablates the recovery in cell viability conferred by iron supplementation in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: The addition of the mitochondrial respiratory chain complex III inhibitor antimycin A to bafilomycin-treated iron-supplemented fibroblasts ablated the recovery in cell viability conferred by the iron supplementation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation and antimycin A treatment (Figure 4D).

claim: Antimycin A treatment ablates the recovery in cell viability conferred by iron supplementation in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts.
source: A similar result was observed in saliphe-treated (Figure 4E) and in deferoxamine-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation and antimycin A treatment (Figure 4E).

claim: Antimycin A treatment ablates the recovery in cell viability conferred by iron supplementation in deferoxamine-treated fibroblasts.
source: A similar result was observed in saliphe-treated (Figure 4E) and in deferoxamine-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in deferoxamine-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation and antimycin A treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Bafilomycin-induced cell death is not apoptotic as shown by absence of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP.
source: We could not detect either cleaved caspase-3 or cleaved PARP in bafilomycin- (Figure 4F) or saliphe-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), despite they were readily detectable in cells treated with the apoptosis inducer staurosporine.
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4F).

claim: Saliphenylhalamide-induced cell death is not apoptotic as shown by absence of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP.
source: We could not detect either cleaved caspase-3 or cleaved PARP in bafilomycin- (Figure 4F) or saliphe-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), despite they were readily detectable in cells treated with the apoptosis inducer staurosporine.
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Pan-caspase inhibitor ZVAD has no attenuating effect on cell death in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.
source: Accordingly, pan-caspase inhibitor ZVAD had no attenuating effect on cell death in bafilomycin- or saliphe-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4G), further supporting that the cell death in these conditions is not apoptotic.
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with ZVAD treatment (Figure 4G).

claim: Pan-caspase inhibitor ZVAD has no attenuating effect on cell death in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts.
source: Accordingly, pan-caspase inhibitor ZVAD had no attenuating effect on cell death in bafilomycin- or saliphe-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4G), further supporting that the cell death in these conditions is not apoptotic.
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with ZVAD treatment (Figure 4G).

claim: Necrostatin-1s has no effect on cell death caused by v-ATPase inhibition.
source: Necrostatin-1s, which can decrease necroptotic cell death by inhibiting RIP1 kinase, had no effect on the cell death caused by v-ATPase inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with necrostatin-1s treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Ferrostatin has no effect on v-ATPase inhibition-induced cell death.
source: Ferrostatin, an inhibitor of ferroptosis, also had no effect on v-ATPase inhibition-induced cell death (Figure 4H), despite it effectively inhibited cell death triggered by the ferroptosis inducer erastin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin or saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with ferrostatin treatment (Figure 4H).

claim: Deferoxamine treatment results in increased Tnfa expression in primary cortical neurons.
source: We first observed the expression of tumor necrosis α (Tnfa) and found a robust increase in its transcript levels in deferoxamine-treated primary neurons (Figure 4I).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tnfa in deferoxamine-treated primary neurons (Figure 4I).

claim: Deferoxamine treatment results in increased expression of innate immune regulators in primary cortical neurons.
source: We then measured the transcript levels of innate immune regulators such as Tlr9, Myd88, Irf7, Stat1 and Stat2, which were all robustly up-regulated in deferoxamine-treated cortical neurons (Figure 4J).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tlr9, Myd88, Irf7, Stat1, and Stat2 in deferoxamine-treated primary neurons (Figure 4J).

claim: Deferoxamine treatment results in increased expression of interferon-stimulated genes in primary cortical neurons.
source: Accordingly, the expression of other downstream interferon-stimulated genes such as Cxcl10, Isg15, Ifit1, Ifit3 and Ifi44 was also strongly induced in deferoxamine-treated neurons (Figure 4K).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Cxcl10, Isg15, Ifit1, Ifit3, and Ifi44 in deferoxamine-treated primary neurons (Figure 4K).

claim: Gaa-KO mouse cortex shows increased Tfrc transcript levels at 6 and 12 months of age.
source: We observed a robust increase in the transcript levels of Tfrc in the cortex of 6- and 12-month-old mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfrc in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 6 and 12 months (Figure 5A).

claim: Gaa-KO mouse cortex shows decreased FTL1 protein levels at 6 and 12 months of age.
source: Ferritin light chain protein levels were down-regulated both at 6- and 12 months (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of FTL1 in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 6 and 12 months (Figure 5B).

claim: Gaa-KO mouse cortex shows increased HIF-1α protein levels at 6 and 12 months of age.
source: To further probe the functional consequences of iron-deficiency in the Gaa-KO brain, we also tested if HIF-1α was accumulating, by western blot, and found an increase in its levels in Gaa-KO cortex both at 6- and 12 months (Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of HIF-1α in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 6 and 12 months (Figure 5C).

claim: Gaa-KO mouse cortex shows decreased complex IV activity.
source: Furthermore, mitochondrial iron availability was also affected, as the activity of complex IV, which is dependent on Fe, was decreased in Gaa-KO cortex (Figure 5D), while the activity of complex V (loading control) was similar between WT and KO mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: Shown by native complex IV activity staining in mitochondria purified from Gaa-KO mouse cortex (Figure 5D).

claim: Gaa-KO mouse brain shows decreased T2 relaxation time of water protons in thalamus, striatum, and cerebral cortex.
source: For this, we analyzed the thalamus, striatum and cerebral cortex, and in all three regions we found a decrease in the T2 relaxation time of water protons (Table 1), which is highly correlated with reduced labile iron pool levels (Vymazal et al., 1993).
evidence: Shown by MRI measurements in Gaa-KO mice at 6 and 12 months (Table 1).

claim: Gaa-KO mouse brain shows reduced levels of choline-containing compounds by MRS.
source: Interestingly, we also observed by MRS, reduced levels of choline-containing compounds, which may be due slow turnover of phosphatidylcholine, further suggesting impaired myelination (Figure 5E–F and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Shown by MRS measurements in Gaa-KO mice at 6 and 12 months (Figure 5E-F).

claim: Gaa-KO mouse cortex shows decreased protein levels of myelination-related proteins PLP and MBP.
source: We therefore tested whether myelination (which is also a Fe-dependent process) was affected in the Gaa-KO cortex. We observed that the abundance of myelination-related proteins such as proteolipid protein (PLP) and myelin basic protein (MBP) was decreased in Gaa-KO cortical homogenates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of PLP and MBP in Gaa-KO mouse cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

claim: RNA sequencing of Gaa-KO mouse cortex identified 1779 differentially expressed genes.
source: We identified 1779 differentially expressed genes (adjusted p value < 0.05; fold change >2.0), of which 996 were up-regulated and 783 were down-regulated in Gaa-KO cortices.
evidence: Shown by RNA sequencing analysis of Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 12 months.

claim: The most significantly changed transcripts in Gaa-KO cortex include Gaa and proteins related to immune responses.
source: The most significantly changed transcripts were Gaa (as expected) and several proteins related to immune responses, particularly complement activation, macrophage infiltration and genes induced by interferon signaling (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown by RNA sequencing analysis of Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 12 months (Figure 6B).

claim: Several pathways related to inflammation are enriched in the Gaa-KO cortex dataset.
source: Accordingly, several pathways related to inflammation were found enriched in the Gaa-KO dataset (Figure 6C).
evidence: Shown by pathway analysis of RNA sequencing data from Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 12 months (Figure 6C).

claim: Irf7 and Irf3 are predicted as the two most active transcription factors in Gaa-KO cortex.
source: We then determined which upstream regulators (specifically, transcription factors) were affected in the Gaa-KO cortex, and found that the interferon regulatory factors Irf7 and Irf3 were predicted as the two most active transcription factors (Figure 6D).
evidence: Shown by upstream regulator analysis of RNA sequencing data from Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 12 months (Figure 6D).

claim: 17 out of 20 Irf7 targets are robustly up-regulated in Gaa-KO cortex.
source: Thus, we focused on the target genes of Irf7, and using the Gaa-KO cortex transcriptome data we observed that 17 out of 20 Irf7 targets in the Gaa-KO brain were robustly up-regulated (Figure 6E).
evidence: Shown by analysis of Irf7 target genes in RNA sequencing data from Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 12 months (Figure 6E).

claim: Most interferon-stimulated genes and their regulators are up-regulated in Gaa-KO cortex at 2, 6, and 12 months of age.
source: We measured by qPCR the transcript levels of several transcripts regulated by Irf7, most of which were up-regulated in the Gaa-KO brain at 2, 6 and 12 months of age (Figure 6F).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of interferon-stimulated genes in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2, 6, and 12 months (Figure 6F).

claim: Stat1 is up-regulated only at 12 months in Gaa-KO cortex.
source: The exception was Stat1, which was up-regulated only at 12 months.
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Stat1 in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2, 6, and 12 months (Figure 6F).

claim: Gaa-KO cortex shows increased GFAP protein levels at 6 and 12 months of age.
source: We observed an increase in GFAP protein levels in GAA-KO cortex at 6 and 12 months (Figure 6G), by western blot.
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of GFAP in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 6 and 12 months (Figure 6G).

claim: Gaa-KO cortex shows increased number of GFAP-positive cells at 6 months of age.
source: Staining of tissue sections against GFAP protein in the 6 month GAA-KO cortex yielded similar results (Figure 6H).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence staining of GFAP in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 6 months (Figure 6H).

claim: Gaa-KO cortex shows age-dependent decline in mtDNA copy number from 0 to 12 months of age.
source: We observed a reduction in mtDNA of about 20% in newborn mice, 25% at 2 months, and a robust decrease of ~50–60% in 6- and 12 month old Gaa-KO cortices (Figure 7A).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 0, 2, 6, and 12 months (Figure 7A).

claim: Gaa-KO cortex shows reduced TFAM protein levels at 6 months of age.
source: Notably, the protein levels of TFAM, a key protein for mtDNA replication, transcription and maintenance, were reduced by ~50% in the 6 month-old Gaa-KO cortex (Figure 7B).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of TFAM in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 6 months (Figure 7B).

claim: Tfam transcript levels are only 20% down in Gaa-KO brain.
source: The decrease in TFAM protein levels cannot be explained only by decreased transcription, since Tfam transcript levels are only 20% down in the Gaa-KO brain (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfam in Gaa-KO mouse cortex (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Deferoxamine treatment results in ~40% reduction in mtDNA copy number in fibroblasts.
source: We first measured mtDNA copy number in WT fibroblasts treated with the lysosomal iron chelator deferoxamine, and observed a reduction of ~40% in mtDNA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in deferoxamine-treated fibroblasts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Deferoxamine treatment results in ~40% reduction in mtDNA copy number in primary cortical neurons.
source: A similar result was obtained by deferoxamine treatment of primary cortical neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in deferoxamine-treated primary neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Irp1-/- and Irp2-/- fibroblasts show ~40% reduced mtDNA copy number compared to WT.
source: The mtDNA copy number in the Irp1-/- and Irp2-/-KO fibroblasts was ~40% reduced compared to WT (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in Irp1-/- and Irp2-/- fibroblasts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Gaa-KO fibroblasts show ~40% loss of mtDNA.
source: To this end, we used fibroblasts obtained from Gaa-KO and respective WT littermates, and observed a loss of ~40% mtDNA in Gaa-KO (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Gaa-KO fibroblasts show decreased TFAM protein levels.
source: Notably, the protein levels of TFAM were also decreased in Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of TFAM in Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Fe-citrate supplementation increases mtDNA copy number to control values in Gaa-KO fibroblasts.
source: Therefore, we supplemented the cell medium with Fe-citrate, and observed that the mtDNA copy number increased in iron-supplemented Gaa-KO fibroblasts to control values (Figure 7C).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in Gaa-KO fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 7C).

claim: Iron-enriched diet rescues mtDNA copy number defects in 2-month-old Gaa-KO mice.
source: While the GAA-KO mice treated with the control Na-citrate diet showed a ~ 20% decrease in mtDNA in cortex relative to the WT littermates, the Gaa-KO cohort fed iron-enriched chow had mtDNA copy number similar to the WT mice (Figure 7D).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2 months with iron-enriched diet (Figure 7D).

claim: Iron-enriched diet dampens increased expression of innate immune response genes in 2-month-old Gaa-KO mice.
source: So, we analyzed the transcript levels of interferon-stimulated genes and those of their regulators in the cortex of 2 month old mice in Fe-enriched or control diet, and observed that in the iron-supplemented Gaa-KO mice the inflammatory response was ablated (Figure 7E).
evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of interferon-stimulated genes in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2 months with iron-enriched diet (Figure 7E).

claim: Iron-enriched diet decreases GFAP and TNFα protein levels in 2-month-old Gaa-KO cortex.
source: Furthermore, we observed that the protein levels of GFAP and of the inflammatory mediator TNFα were also decreased by the iron-supplementation in the Gaa-KO cortex (Figure 7F).
evidence: Shown by immunoblots of GFAP and TNFα in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2 months with iron-enriched diet (Figure 7F).

claim: Iron-enriched diet normalizes cytokine levels in 2-month-old Gaa-KO cortex.
source: While we barely could observe TNFα, interferon gamma (IFNγ) as well as the cytokines CXCL9, CXCL10, CXCL11, IL-1α, IL-16 in wild type mice, these proteins were significantly increased in the cortices of Gaa-KO fed standard chow, but were normalized to the barely detectable WT levels in the iron-supplemented mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: Shown by cytokine array measurements in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2 months with iron-enriched diet (Figure 7G).

claim: Iron-enriched diet normalizes stride length in 2-month-old Gaa-KO mice.
source: We observed that several parameters were affected in the Gaa-KO already at 2 months of age, particularly the stride length, which was decreased in the Gaa-KO mice (Figure 7H). This is an indication of gait disorder (Fernagut et al., 2002), suggesting that the Gaa-KO mice may have motor impairments. Notably, the Gaa-KO mice supplemented with iron showed a normalization of the stride length (Figure 7H).
evidence: Shown by DigiGait analysis in Gaa-KO mice at 2 months with iron-enriched diet (Figure 7H).

claim: Decreased stride length in Gaa-KO mice is an indication of gait disorder.
source: This is an indication of gait disorder (Fernagut et al., 2002), suggesting that the Gaa-KO mice may have motor impairments.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fernagut et al., 2002.

claim: Impaired lysosomal acidification links to mitochondrial malfunction and inflammation in vivo.
source: Our results highlight a novel mechanism linking impaired lysosomal acidification, mitochondrial malfunction and inflammation in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by the comprehensive data showing iron deficiency, mitochondrial dysfunction, mtDNA instability, and inflammation in Gaa-KO mice, all corrected by iron supplementation.

claim: Iron release from (endo)lysosomes to cytoplasm requires acidic pH.
source: We show here that iron release from (endo)lysosomes to cytoplasm requires acidic pH.
evidence: Demonstrated by increased lysosomal iron and decreased cytoplasmic iron in bafilomycin-treated cells (Figure 1F, I).

claim: Fe3+ obtained from ferritinophagy, mitophagy or transferrin endocytosis cannot be reduced to Fe2+ when lysosomes are not properly acidified.
source: When the (endo)lysosomes are not properly acidified, Fe3+ obtained from ferritinophagy, mitophagy or transferrin endocytosis cannot be reduced to Fe2+.
evidence: Based on the known function of STEAP3 requiring acidic pH and the observed accumulation of Fe3+ in Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 2I).

claim: STEAP3 has an optimal acidic pH for Fe3+ reduction.
source: This reduction is catalyzed by the ferroreductase STEAP3, which has an optimal acidic pH (Lambe et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lambe et al., 2009.

claim: Only Fe2+ can be exported from lysosomes via DMT1 or MCOLN1.
source: The inability to reduce Fe3+ to Fe2+ results in the accumulation of Fe3+ in the lysosomes, since only Fe2+ can be exported via the channels divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) or mucolipin-1 (MCOLN1) (Dong et al., 2008; Touret et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2008 and Touret et al., 2003.

claim: Cytoplasmic Fe levels determine when the cellular iron deficiency response is activated.
source: The proteins that sense cellular iron function are located in the cytoplasm, implying that cytoplasmic Fe levels determine when the cellular iron deficiency response is activated.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of IRP1 and IRP2 function in the cytoplasm.

claim: Low Fe levels result in the conversion of aconitase in IRP1 and stabilization of IRP2.
source: Low Fe levels result in the conversion of aconitase in IRP1 and stabilization of IRP2 (Rouault, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rouault, 2015.

claim: IRP1 and IRP2 promote iron mobilization and uptake while repressing storage and export.
source: Together, these proteins promote iron mobilization and uptake, while repressing its storage and export from the cell.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of IRP function.

claim: The iron homeostatic program requires functional lysosomes.
source: We show here that this program of iron homeostasis requires functional lysosomes.
evidence: Demonstrated by iron deficiency response in cells with impaired lysosomal acidification.

claim: Iron deficiency caused by v-ATPase inhibition results in cell death.
source: Accordingly, inhibition of lysosomal v-ATPase and the consequent iron deficiency result in cell death.
evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin or saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4A-B).

claim: The main contributor to cell death caused by impaired lysosomal acidification is iron deficiency.
source: Nevertheless, the simple repletion of iron through an (endo)lysosome-independent pathway was sufficient to restore cell proliferation almost to control levels. Therefore, the main contributor to cell death caused by impaired (endo)lysosomal acidification seems to be iron deficiency.
evidence: Demonstrated by Fe-citrate supplementation restoring cell viability in v-ATPase inhibitor-treated cells (Figure 4C).

claim: The cell death caused by iron deficiency is non-apoptotic and likely contributes to inflammation in vivo.
source: We determined that the cell death caused by iron deficiency is non-apoptotic, which likely contributes to the inflammation observed in vivo in the brain of a mouse model of lysosomal malfunction (Gaa-KO).
evidence: Shown by absence of apoptotic markers in bafilomycin-treated cells (Figure 4F-G) and inflammation in Gaa-KO brain (Figure 6).

claim: The inflammation trigger caused by iron deficiency is cell-intrinsic.
source: While we cannot exclude the possibility that neuronal cell death in culture was sensed by astrocytes or glia that are present in the culture (primary neurons typically have a small number of co-cultured astrocytes and microglia), our results suggest that the inflammation trigger is cell-intrinsic.
evidence: Suggested by increased inflammatory gene expression in deferoxamine-treated primary neurons (Figure 4I-K).

claim: mtDNA replication relies mostly on cytoplasmic dNTP production.
source: There is no dedicated de novo production of dNTPs for mtDNA synthesis, and mtDNA replication relies mostly on the cytoplasmic dNTP production (Copeland, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Copeland, 2012.

claim: Ribonucleotide reductase has Fe in its active center.
source: A key step in dNTP production is catalyzed by the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase, a heterodimeric protein that has Fe in its active center (Puig et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Puig et al., 2017.

claim: Decreased availability of dNTPs is a known cause of mtDNA instability.
source: Decreased availability of dNTPs is a known cause of mtDNA instability, which in turn is an inflammatory trigger.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Iron deficiency perturbs mtDNA homeostasis regardless of cell type or mechanism.
source: We show here that iron deficiency perturbs mtDNA homeostasis, regardless of the cell type (fibroblasts, neurons) or the mechanism (genetic, pharmacologic) that leads to iron deficiency.
evidence: Demonstrated by decreased mtDNA in deferoxamine-treated cells, Irp1/2-KO cells, and Gaa-KO cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-E).

claim: The levels of mtDNA decrease sharply in iron deficiency.
source: We also show here that the levels of mtDNA decrease sharply in iron deficiency.
evidence: Demonstrated by decreased mtDNA in various iron deficiency models (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-E).

claim: In Tfam+/- mice, mtDNA instability triggers interferon-dependent signaling that culminates in potent inflammatory responses.
source: In the Tfam+/- mice, mtDNA instability triggers interferon-dependent signaling that culminates in potent inflammatory responses (West et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to West et al., 2015.

claim: Iron deficiency is associated with mtDNA instability and inflammation in vitro and in vivo.
source: We show here that iron deficiency, either caused by iron chelation, genetic ablation of Irp1 or Irp2, or genetic defects impairing lysosomal acidification, is associated both with mtDNA instability and inflammation, in vitro and, importantly, in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by decreased mtDNA and increased inflammatory markers in various iron deficiency models (Figures 6, 7).

claim: Supplying iron via an endo/lysosome-independent route resolves iron deficiency response, loss of mtDNA, and inflammatory signaling.
source: Notably, supplying iron via an endo/lysosome-independent route resolved the iron deficiency response, the loss of mtDNA and the inflammatory signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by Fe-citrate supplementation rescuing these phenotypes in cells and iron-enriched diet rescuing them in mice (Figures 2-4, 7).

claim: Prolyl hydroxylases catalyze the hydroxylation of HIF-1α.
source: The prolyl hydroxylases are part of the α-ketoglutarate-dependent superfamily, and catalyze the hydroxylation of the α-subunit of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1α).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of HIF-1α regulation.

claim: After hydroxylation, HIF-1α is recognized by VHL and labeled for proteasomal degradation.
source: After hydroxylation, HIF-1α is recognized by the ubiquitin ligase VHL, and labeled for proteasomal degradation (Raimundo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raimundo et al., 2011.

claim: HIF-1α is constitutively expressed and readily degraded under normal conditions.
source: HIF-1α is therefore constitutively expressed and readily degraded under normal conditions, and thus barely detectable (Raimundo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raimundo et al., 2011.

claim: In the absence of VHL or when prolyl hydroxylases are impaired, HIF-1α accumulates and triggers the pseudo-hypoxia response.
source: However, in the absence of VHL or when the function of prolyl hydroxylases is impaired, HIF-1α accumulates and triggers a transcriptional program known as (pseudo-)hypoxia response.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of HIF-1α regulation.

claim: Activation of HIF signaling is a consequence of impaired lysosomal acidification.
source: Therefore, the activation of HIF signaling is a novel consequence of impaired lysosomal acidification (Miles et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miles et al., 2017 and data showing HIF-1α accumulation in v-ATPase inhibitor-treated cells (Figure 1D).

claim: HIF signaling can be activated by mitochondrial malfunction, particularly loss-of-function of fumarate hydratase or succinate dehydrogenase.
source: Notably, HIF signaling can also be activated by mitochondrial malfunction, particularly loss-of-function of the citrate cycle enzymes fumarate hydratase or succinate dehydrogenase, which results in the accumulation of fumarate and succinate, and in the consequent inhibition of the prolyl hydroxylases.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: HIF-1α can be seen as a sensor of the mitochondrial-lysosomal axis.
source: Therefore, HIF-1α can be seen as a sensor of the mitochondrial-lysosomal axis.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing HIF-1α accumulation in response to both lysosomal and mitochondrial dysfunction.

claim: The constitutive silencing of the pseudo-hypoxia response requires both functional lysosomes and functional mitochondria.
source: Reciprocally, it can also be noted that the constitutive silencing of the (pseudo)hypoxia response requires both functional lysosomes and functional mitochondria.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing HIF-1α accumulation when either lysosomes or mitochondria are dysfunctional.

claim: Many genes causing inherited Parkinson's disease are associated with mitochondria or lysosomes/autophagy.
source: For example, many of the genes that cause inherited Parkinson's disease are associated either with mitochondria or lysosomes/autophagy, and therefore the primarily-damaged organelle is likely to promote the secondary impairment of the other.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: This manuscript presents a novel role of mitochondria-lysosome crosstalk in the regulation of central nervous system inflammation in vivo.
source: This manuscript presents a novel role of mitochondria-lysosome crosstalk in the regulation of central nervous system inflammation in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by the comprehensive data showing the link between lysosomal dysfunction, iron deficiency, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation in Gaa-KO mice.
